questions.question: In a domain-separated GRC implementation, how is the domain determined for records that are automatically generated based on their parent object?

options.text: Records are always placed in the global domain
Records inherit the domain of their parent object or creating user's domain
Records are randomly distributed across available domains
Records are placed in the lowest domain in the hierarchy

explanation.correct: Records that are automatically generated either through scheduled jobs or background scripts are domain separated based on their parent object or user domain for all Policy and Compliance objects. Controls, risks, or risk assessments that are auto-generated based on the entities must also be domain separated following this rule.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Auto-generated records do not default to global domain; they follow parent/user domain
Domain assignment is deterministic based on parent object or user, not random
There is no rule to place records in the lowest domain; it's based on parent/user domain

source.excerpt: Records that are automatically generated either through scheduled jobs or background scripts are domain separated based on their parent object or user domain for all Policy and Compliance objects.

questions.question: Which tables are used for reconciliation rules and DO have sys_domain, sys_overrides, and sys_domain_path fields? (Choose three)

options.text: Reconciliation Definition (cmdb_reconciliation_definition)
Identifier (cmdb_identifier)
Datasource Precedence (cmdb_datasource_precedence)
Identifier Entries (cmdb_identifier_entry)
Data Source Staleness Definitions (cmdb_datasource_staleness)

explanation.correct: The reconciliation definition rules that are used during the reconciliation process can be defined for different domains. Tables with sys_domain field include: Reconciliation Definition (cmdb_reconciliation_definition), Datasource Precedence (cmdb_datasource_precedence), and Data Source Staleness Definitions (cmdb_datasource_staleness).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Identifier (cmdb_identifier) does NOT have a sys_domain field; identification rules are global
Identifier Entries (cmdb_identifier_entry) does NOT have a sys_domain field; these are global

source.excerpt: The following tables do have sys_domain, sys_overrides, sys_domain_path fields: Reconciliation Definition (cmdb_reconciliation_definition), Datasource Precedence (cmdb_datasource_precedence), Data Source Staleness Definitions (cmdb_datasource_staleness)

questions.question: How does the CMDB Health dashboard handle domain separation when displaying health failures and scores?

options.text: It shows all CI health data regardless of domain
It aggregates and reports based on user's domain visibility of CIs
It only shows global domain CI health data
Health data must be manually filtered by domain

explanation.correct: If the Domain Support — Domain Extensions Installer plugin is activated, then the CMDB Health dashboard is domain aware. It aggregates and reports health failures and scores based on user's domain visibility of CIs. If domain visibility lets a user see a CI, then the audit rule in that user's domain applies to that CI.

wrongAnswers.explanation: The dashboard respects domain visibility; it does not show all CI data
The dashboard shows data for the user's visible domains, not only global
Domain filtering is automatic based on user visibility, not manual

source.excerpt: The CMDB Health dashboard aggregates and reports health failures and scores based on user's domain visibility of CIs. If domain visibility lets a user see a CI, then the audit rule in that user's domain applies to that CI.

questions.question:
Evaluate the following statements about CMDB Health rules in a domain-separated environment:

Statement 1: Required fields for completeness are based on the class schema defined in System dictionary and are fixed for all domains.

Statement 2: Orphan rules are domain-separated and can be different for different domains.

Which statements are TRUE?

options.text: Statement 1 only
Statement 2 only
Both statements
Neither statement

explanation.correct: Both statements are TRUE. Required fields are based on the class schema defined in the platform's System dictionary and cannot be changed - they are fixed for all domains. Orphan rules are domain-separated; there are different orphan rules for different domains stored in the CMDB Health Orphan Rule [cmdb_health_orphan_rule] table which is domain separated.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Both statements are true; orphan rules ARE domain-separated
Both statements are true; required fields ARE fixed across domains
Both statements are true as documented in CMDB Health domain separation

source.excerpt: Required fields – These are based on the class schema defined in the platform's System dictionary and is fixed for all domains. Orphan – Orphan rules are domain separated; there are different orphan rules for different domains.

questions.question: What happens when a CI is inserted during the identification process and no records are found, regardless of domain separation mode?

options.text: The CI is placed in the global domain
The CI domain ID is the same as the domain ID of the logged-in user's domain
The CI is queued for manual domain assignment
The CI is rejected until a domain is specified

explanation.correct: During matching, if no records are found and a CI is inserted, the CI domain ID is the same as the domain ID of the logged-in user's domain. Domain IDs don't need to be explicitly sent in the input payload of the identification engine APIs; internally, the identification engine uses the current domain ID of the user calling the APIs.

wrongAnswers.explanation: CIs inherit the logged-in user's domain, not automatically the global domain
Domain assignment is automatic based on the logged-in user's domain, not queued for manual assignment
CIs are not rejected; they automatically receive the logged-in user's domain

source.excerpt: During matching, if no records are found and a CI is inserted, the CI domain ID is the same as the domain ID of the logged-in user's domain.

questions.question: Starting with the Tokyo release, how are metric tests from the global domain applied to subdomains in CMDB Health?

options.text: Global domain metric tests are never applied to subdomains
CIs in the global domain are evaluated only against metric tests specified in the global domain
All subdomain tests are applied to global CIs
Metric tests must be manually replicated to each subdomain

explanation.correct: Starting with the Tokyo release, CIs in the global domain are evaluated only against metric tests specified in the global domain. In subdomains, local metric tests are applied only to the CIs in that subdomain and are not applied to the global domain CIs (even though they are visible). This prevents large amounts of duplicated data from subdomain tests on global CIs.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Global metric tests do propagate to subdomains for local CIs, but global CIs are only evaluated by global tests
This was the old behavior before Tokyo; subdomain tests are no longer applied to global CIs
Metric tests propagate automatically; manual replication is not required

source.excerpt: Starting with the Tokyo release, CIs in the global domain are evaluated only against metric tests specified in the global domain. In subdomains, local metric tests are applied only to the CIs in that subdomain and are not applied to the global domain CIs.

questions.question: Which Health Preferences settings are domain-separated and can be configured differently for each domain? (Choose three)

options.text: Global system properties
Failure Threshold
Create Task setting
Task Assignee Group
Dashboard job schedule

explanation.correct: Failure Threshold, Create Task, and Task Assignee Group can be set differently for different domains depending on what is needed in each domain. These settings are stored in the cmdb_health_metric_pref table, which is domain separated.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Global system properties that control CMDB Health are NOT domain separated
There is one dashboard job for each major KPI that runs for all domains; jobs are not domain-separated

source.excerpt: Failure Threshold, Create Task, Task Assignee Group – All these settings can be set differently for different domains depending on what is needed in each domain.

questions.question: An administrator is concerned about long-running CMDB Health dashboard jobs in an environment with many domains. What is the most effective way to reduce job runtime?

options.text: Increase the server memory allocation
Set the Active flag to false for domains that don't need to appear in the dashboard
Reduce the number of CIs in the database
Run the jobs during off-peak hours only

explanation.correct: The Active setting is the most important because it affects how long the jobs run. The more domains with flags set to Active, the longer the jobs take. It's best to select only those domains you wish to be Active and set Active=false for the rest. If there is a large number of domains (>100), the job can take a very long time. Setting Active to false for root domains disables all child domains in the hierarchy.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Memory allocation doesn't address the fundamental issue of processing too many domains
Reducing CIs may not be practical and doesn't address domain-related processing time
Timing doesn't reduce the actual job duration; disabling unnecessary domains does

source.excerpt: Active – This setting is the most important because it affects how long the jobs run. The more domains with flags set to Active, the longer the jobs take. If there is a large number of domains (>100) the job can take a very long time.

questions.question: What is NOT a characteristic of Health inclusion rules in a domain-separated CMDB environment?

options.text: Health inclusion rules are domain separated
Each domain can have its specific health inclusion rules
Rules defined globally are inherited by all sub-domains
Health inclusion rules automatically sync across instances

explanation.correct: Health inclusion rules do NOT automatically sync across instances - this is not a feature of health inclusion rules. However, they ARE domain separated, each domain CAN have specific rules, rules defined globally ARE inherited by sub-domains according to domain structure, and rules can be overridden at any domain or class level.

wrongAnswers.explanation: This statement is TRUE; health inclusion rules are stored in the cmdb_health_config table which is domain separated
This statement is TRUE; each domain can have domain-specific rules
This statement is TRUE; global rules are inherited by sub-domains and can be overridden

source.excerpt: Health inclusion rules are domain separated. The rules are stored in the cmdb_health_config table which is domain separated. Each domain can have its specific health inclusion rules. When a health inclusion rule is defined globally, all sub-domains inherit the rule.

questions.question: Which tables have sys_domain field for domain separation in CMDB Reconciliation?

options.text: Identifier and Identifier Entries tables
Reconciliation Definition and Datasource Precedence tables
All CMDB tables
No tables have domain fields

explanation.correct: Reconciliation Definition (cmdb_reconciliation_definition) and Datasource Precedence (cmdb_datasource_precedence) tables have sys_domain, sys_overrides, and sys_domain_path fields, allowing domain-specific reconciliation rules. Identification rules are always global.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Identifier and Identifier Entries tables don't have sys_domain field - they're always global
Not all CMDB tables have domain fields
Some tables do have domain fields for reconciliation

source.excerpt: The reconciliation definition rules that are used during the reconciliation process can be defined for different domains. For example, the following tables do have sys_domain, sys_overrides, sys_domain_path fields: Reconciliation Definition, Datasource Precedence, Data Source Staleness Definitions.

questions.question: Where are Identification Rules defined in a domain-separated instance?

options.text: Per domain
At the global level only
Per user
Per CI class

explanation.correct: Identification rules and identification inclusion rules are always defined at the global level. The following tables don't have a sys_domain field: Identifier (cmdb_identifier), Identifier Entries (cmdb_identifier_entry), Related Entries (cmdb_related_entry), Identification Inclusion Rules (cmdb_ie_active_config).

wrongAnswers.explanation: Identification rules cannot be domain-specific
Identification rules are not per-user
While rules apply to CI classes, the rules themselves are global

source.excerpt: The identification rules and identification inclusion rules used during the identification process are always defined at the global level. For example, the following tables don't have a sys_domain field: Identifier, Identifier Entries, Related Entries, Identification Inclusion Rules.

questions.question: An MSP needs different CI data staleness rules for different customer domains. Which table should be configured?

options.text: cmdb_identifier
cmdb_datasource_staleness
cmdb_identifier_entry
cmdb_ie_active_config

explanation.correct: The Data Source Staleness Definitions table (cmdb_datasource_staleness) has sys_domain field and can be configured per domain to define different staleness rules for each customer's CIs.

wrongAnswers.explanation: cmdb_identifier is for identification rules which are global
cmdb_identifier_entry is for identification which is global
This is for identification inclusion rules which are global

source.excerpt: The following tables do have sys_domain, sys_overrides, sys_domain_path fields: Reconciliation Definition (cmdb_reconciliation_definition), Datasource Precedence (cmdb_datasource_precedence), Data Source Staleness Definitions (cmdb_datasource_staleness).

questions.question: How does the domain_path field work in domain-separated tables?

options.text: It stores the user's navigation history
It contains the full path from the root domain to the record's domain, enabling efficient domain hierarchy queries
It stores the file path for attachments
It records the URL path for the record

explanation.correct: The sys_domain_path field stores the complete hierarchy path (e.g., /global/TOP/CustomerA/) enabling the system to efficiently determine domain visibility and inheritance.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Navigation history is tracked separately from domain paths
Attachment paths use different fields
URL paths are generated dynamically, not stored in sys_domain_path

questions.question: A service provider needs to import CI data for multiple tenants via a single data source. How should they handle domain assignment during import?

options.text: Import all data to global and manually reassign later
Use transform map scripts to set the sys_domain field based on tenant identifiers in the source data
Create separate import sets for each tenant
Domain assignment happens automatically

explanation.correct: Transform map scripts can programmatically set the sys_domain field during import based on tenant identifiers in the source data, ensuring correct domain assignment at import time.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Importing to global requires additional manual effort and risks data exposure
While possible, separate imports are less efficient than using transform scripts for domain routing
Domain assignment requires explicit configuration; it doesn't happen automatically for imported data

questions.question: In CMDB domain separation, what is the purpose of the 'containment' domain separation mode for IRE?

options.text: It quarantines infected CIs
It ensures CIs are only matched within their own domain during identification, preventing cross-domain CI matching
It limits the size of the CMDB
It encrypts CI data within domains

explanation.correct: Containment mode (also known as strict mode) ensures that CI identification only matches records within the same domain, preventing a CI in one tenant's domain from matching with another tenant's CIs.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Containment refers to domain boundary enforcement, not security quarantine
CMDB size is managed through other mechanisms
Encryption is handled by separate security features

questions.question: An MSP notices that CMDB Health scores are inconsistent across tenant domains. What is the MOST likely explanation?

options.text: CMDB Health doesn't work with domain separation
Each domain can have different Health Preferences and metric configurations, leading to different scoring criteria
The CMDB Health plugin needs to be reinstalled
Only the global domain can have health scores

explanation.correct: CMDB Health preferences (like staleness thresholds and inclusion rules) are domain-separated, meaning each domain can have different configurations that produce different scores.

wrongAnswers.explanation: CMDB Health is supported with domain separation
Plugin reinstallation doesn't address domain-specific configuration differences
Health scores are calculated per domain when domain separation is active

questions.question: Which table is used to define domain visibility rules in ServiceNow?

options.text: sys_user_group
domain_table_access
sys_db_object
sys_user_role

explanation.correct: The domain_table_access table defines which domains have visibility to records in specific tables, controlling cross-domain data access beyond the default hierarchy-based visibility.

wrongAnswers.explanation: sys_user_group manages groups, not domain visibility rules
sys_db_object defines table metadata, not domain access rules
sys_user_role manages roles, not domain visibility

questions.question: What is the sys_overrides field used for in domain separation?

options.text: To override system security
To allow a domain-specific record to override a parent domain record with the same key values
To bypass approval workflows
To override user session timeouts

explanation.correct: The sys_overrides field enables domain-specific customization by allowing a child domain record to override a parent domain record, such as having a domain-specific business rule override a global one.

wrongAnswers.explanation: sys_overrides is for domain record inheritance, not security bypass
Approval workflows use different override mechanisms
Session timeouts are managed by system properties

questions.question: What happens to CMDB configuration items when domain separation is enabled?

options.text: All CIs are automatically duplicated for each domain
CIs can be assigned to specific domains using the sys_domain field
CMDB does not support domain separation
CIs are always visible across all domains regardless of separation

explanation.correct: When domain separation is enabled, CMDB configuration items can be assigned to specific domains using the sys_domain field, controlling which tenants can see which CIs.

wrongAnswers.explanation: CIs are not automatically duplicated; they are assigned to domains
CMDB fully supports domain separation
Domain separation restricts CI visibility based on domain assignment

questions.question: Which approach is recommended for managing users who need access to multiple domains?

options.text: Create duplicate user accounts in each domain
Assign the user to the global domain
Use domain override records to grant cross-domain access
Elevate the user to the admin role

explanation.correct: Domain override records allow specific users to access records in domains other than their own without creating duplicates or granting excessive privileges.

wrongAnswers.explanation: Duplicate accounts create management overhead and are not recommended
Assigning to global domain may grant too broad access
Admin role is excessive and violates least-privilege principle
